claim: In the primary visual cortex (V1) of mice, synapses between excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons tend to be stronger for neurons that respond to similar stimulus features.
source: In the primary visual cortex (V1) of mice, synapses between excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons tend to be stronger for neurons that respond to similar stimulus features, although these neurons are not topographically arranged according to their stimulus preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental findings in mouse V1.

claim: Pyramidal neurons and PV interneurons in mouse V1 are not topographically arranged according to their stimulus preference.
source: In the primary visual cortex (V1) of mice, synapses between excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons tend to be stronger for neurons that respond to similar stimulus features, although these neurons are not topographically arranged according to their stimulus preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental findings in mouse V1.

claim: Activity-dependent synaptic plasticity on input and output synapses of PV interneurons generates a circuit structure that is consistent with mouse V1.
source: Here, we show that activity-dependent synaptic plasticity on input and output synapses of PV interneurons generates a circuit structure that is consistent with mouse V1.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both input and output plasticity must act in synergy to form E/I assemblies.
source: Computational modeling reveals that both forms of plasticity must act in synergy to form the observed E/I assemblies.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results, specifically knock-out experiments.

claim: E/I assemblies produce a stimulus-specific competition between pyramidal neurons.
source: Once established, these assemblies produce a stimulus-specific competition between pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation experiments in the computational model.

claim: Inhibition serves to stabilize recurrent excitatory feedback loops in neuronal circuits.
source: Aside from the classical perspective that inhibition serves to stabilize recurrent excitatory feedback loops in neuronal circuits (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Brunel, 2000; Murphy and Miller, 2009; Sprekeler, 2017), it is increasingly recognised as an active player in cortical computation (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Priebe and Ferster, 2008; Rubin et al., 2015; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Letzkus et al., 2011; Adesnik et al., 2012; Hennequin et al., 2014; Phillips et al., 2017; Barron et al., 2016; Barron et al., 2017; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition is increasingly recognised as an active player in cortical computation.
source: Aside from the classical perspective that inhibition serves to stabilize recurrent excitatory feedback loops in neuronal circuits (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Brunel, 2000; Murphy and Miller, 2009; Sprekeler, 2017), it is increasingly recognised as an active player in cortical computation (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Priebe and Ferster, 2008; Rubin et al., 2015; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Letzkus et al., 2011; Adesnik et al., 2012; Hennequin et al., 2014; Phillips et al., 2017; Barron et al., 2016; Barron et al., 2017; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated in their response to stimuli within cortical neurons.
source: Within cortical neurons, excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated in their response to stimuli (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2011; Bhatia et al., 2019), in time (Okun and Lampl, 2008; Dipoppa et al., 2018) and across neurons (Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated in time within cortical neurons.
source: Within cortical neurons, excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated in their response to stimuli (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2011; Bhatia et al., 2019), in time (Okun and Lampl, 2008; Dipoppa et al., 2018) and across neurons (Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated across neurons.
source: Within cortical neurons, excitatory and inhibitory currents are often highly correlated in their response to stimuli (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2011; Bhatia et al., 2019), in time (Okun and Lampl, 2008; Dipoppa et al., 2018) and across neurons (Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In topographically organised sensory areas such as cat primary visual cortex (V1), co-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory currents with respect to sensory stimuli could be a natural consequence of local feedback inhibition.
source: In topographically organised sensory areas such as cat primary visual cortex (V1), the co-tuning with respect to sensory stimuli could be a natural consequence of local feedback inhibition and does not impose strong constraints on inhibitory circuitry (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Co-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory currents in feedforward inhibition was suggested to arise from homeostatic synaptic plasticity in GABAergic synapses.
source: In the case of feedforward inhibition, co-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory currents was suggested to arise from homeostatic synaptic plasticity in GABAergic synapses (Vogels et al., 2011; Clopath et al., 2016; Weber and Sprekeler, 2018; Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: V1 of rodents has poor feature topography.
source: In sensory areas with poor feature topography, such as V1 of rodents (Ohki et al., 2005), feedback inhibition has been hypothesised to be largely unspecific for stimulus features, a property inferred from the dense connectivity (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer and Yuste, 2011) and reliable presence of synapses connecting pyramidal (Pyr) neurons to inhibitory interneurons with dissimilar stimulus tuning (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Bock et al., 2011; Hofer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Feedback inhibition in rodent V1 has been hypothesised to be largely unspecific for stimulus features.
source: In sensory areas with poor feature topography, such as V1 of rodents (Ohki et al., 2005), feedback inhibition has been hypothesised to be largely unspecific for stimulus features, a property inferred from the dense connectivity (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer and Yuste, 2011) and reliable presence of synapses connecting pyramidal (Pyr) neurons to inhibitory interneurons with dissimilar stimulus tuning (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Bock et al., 2011; Hofer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work and inference from connectivity patterns.

claim: In mouse V1, although the presence of synaptic connections between Pyr cells and PV interneurons is independent of their respective stimulus responses, the efficacy of those synapses is correlated with their response similarity.
source: In mouse V1, Znamenskiy et al., 2018 report that although the presence of synaptic connections between Pyr cells and parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons is independent of their respective stimulus responses, the efficacy of those synapses is correlated with their response similarity, both in PV → Pyr and in Pyr → PV connections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work by Znamenskiy et al., 2018.

claim: The efficacy of PV → Pyr synapses is correlated with response similarity in mouse V1.
source: In mouse V1, Znamenskiy et al., 2018 report that although the presence of synaptic connections between Pyr cells and parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons is independent of their respective stimulus responses, the efficacy of those synapses is correlated with their response similarity, both in PV → Pyr and in Pyr → PV connections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work by Znamenskiy et al., 2018.

claim: The efficacy of Pyr → PV synapses is correlated with response similarity in mouse V1.
source: In mouse V1, Znamenskiy et al., 2018 report that although the presence of synaptic connections between Pyr cells and parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons is independent of their respective stimulus responses, the efficacy of those synapses is correlated with their response similarity, both in PV → Pyr and in Pyr → PV connections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work by Znamenskiy et al., 2018.

claim: Mutual preferences in synaptic organisation between Pyr and PV neurons suggest that feedback inhibition may be more stimulus-specific than previously thought.
source: These mutual preferences in synaptic organisation suggest that feedback inhibition may be more stimulus-specific than previously thought and that Pyr and PV neurons form specialised—albeit potentially overlapping—excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) assemblies (Chenkov et al., 2017; Yoshimura et al., 2005; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observed synaptic organization patterns, supported by citations.

claim: Pyr and PV neurons form specialised excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) assemblies.
source: These mutual preferences in synaptic organisation suggest that feedback inhibition may be more stimulus-specific than previously thought and that Pyr and PV neurons form specialised—albeit potentially overlapping—excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) assemblies (Chenkov et al., 2017; Yoshimura et al., 2005; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and inference from synaptic organization.

claim: The presence of E/I assemblies suggests the need for an activity-dependent mechanism for their formation and/or refinement.
source: While the presence of such E/I assemblies (Znamenskiy et al., 2018; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018) suggests the need for an activity-dependent mechanism for their formation and/or refinement (Khan et al., 2018; Najafi et al., 2020), the requirements such a mechanism must fulfil remain unresolved.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the existence of E/I assemblies, supported by citations.

claim: Each excitatory neuron receives external excitatory input that is tuned to orientation, temporal frequency and spatial frequency.
source: To endow the excitatory neurons with a stimulus tuning similar to Pyr cells in layer 2/3 of mouse V1 (Znamenskiy et al., 2018), each excitatory neuron receives external excitatory input that is tuned to orientation, temporal frequency and spatial frequency (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The preferred stimuli of the Pyr neurons cover the stimulus space evenly.
source: The preferred stimuli of the Pyr neurons cover the stimulus space evenly.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design.

claim: Inhibitory neurons receive external inputs without stimulus tuning.
source: Because we are interested under which conditions feedback inhibition can acquire a stimulus selectivity, inhibitory neurons receive external inputs without stimulus tuning, but are recurrently connected to Pyr neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design.

claim: Pyr neurons are preferentially connected to other Pyr neurons with similar stimulus tuning.
source: While the network has no stimulus topography, Pyr neurons are preferentially connected to other Pyr neurons with similar stimulus tuning (Hofer et al., 2011; Cossell et al., 2015), and connection strength is proportional to the signal correlation of their external inputs.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design, supported by citations to experimental findings.

claim: Connection strength between Pyr neurons is proportional to the signal correlation of their external inputs.
source: While the network has no stimulus topography, Pyr neurons are preferentially connected to other Pyr neurons with similar stimulus tuning (Hofer et al., 2011; Cossell et al., 2015), and connection strength is proportional to the signal correlation of their external inputs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design.

claim: Before learning, interneurons show poor stimulus selectivity.
source: Before learning, interneurons show poor stimulus selectivity (Figure 1c), in line with the notion that in a random network, interneurons pool over many Pyr neurons with different stimulus tuning (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c and citation to previous work.

claim: By the end of learning, interneurons have developed a pronounced stimulus tuning, albeit weaker than that of Pyr neurons.
source: By the end of learning, interneurons have developed a pronounced stimulus tuning, albeit weaker than that of Pyr neurons (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1c and 1d.

claim: Interneurons form strong bidirectional connections preferentially with Pyr neurons with a similar stimulus tuning.
source: Interneurons form strong bidirectional connections preferentially with Pyr neurons with a similar stimulus tuning, whereas connections between Pyr-PV pairs with dissimilar stimulus tuning are weaker (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: Connections between Pyr-PV pairs with dissimilar stimulus tuning are weaker.
source: Interneurons form strong bidirectional connections preferentially with Pyr neurons with a similar stimulus tuning, whereas connections between Pyr-PV pairs with dissimilar stimulus tuning are weaker (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: Both the efficacy of PV input and output connections are highly correlated with the response similarity of the associated Pyr neurons and interneurons.
source: Both the efficacy of PV input and output connections are highly correlated with the response similarity (RS) (see 'Materials and methods') of the associated Pyr neurons and interneurons (Figure 1e, left and centre).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: For bidirectionally connected cell pairs, the efficacies of the respective input and output connections are highly correlated.
source: For bidirectionally connected cell pairs, the efficacies of the respective input and output connections are highly correlated (Figure 1e, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The stimulus tuning of the inhibitory inputs onto the Pyr cells closely resembles that of the excitatory inputs after learning.
source: The stimulus tuning of the inhibitory inputs onto the Pyr cells—initially flat—closely resembles that of the excitatory inputs after learning (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Tan et al., 2011), that is, the network develops a precise E/I balance (Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citations.

claim: The network develops a precise E/I balance.
source: The stimulus tuning of the inhibitory inputs onto the Pyr cells—initially flat—closely resembles that of the excitatory inputs after learning (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Tan et al., 2011), that is, the network develops a precise E/I balance (Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citations.

claim: The optimal gradient rules produce very similar results to the local approximations.
source: Finally, the optimal gradient rules produce very similar results to the local approximations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Over the course of learning, the weight updates by the approximate rules align to the updates that would result from the gradient rules.
source: Over the course of learning, the weight updates by the approximate rules align to the updates that would result from the gradient rules (Figure 1g, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), presumably by a mechanism akin to feedback alignment (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Akrout et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and citations.

claim: When output plasticity is knocked out but input plasticity is kept intact, the network fails to develop E/I assemblies and a stimulus-specific E/I balance.
source: When we knock out output plasticity but keep input plasticity intact, the network fails to develop E/I assemblies and a stimulus-specific E/I balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by knock-out experiment results in the model.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory currents in Pyr neurons are poorly co-tuned when output plasticity is knocked out.
source: Importantly, excitatory and inhibitory currents in Pyr neurons are poorly co-tuned (Figure 2c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Feedback inhibition remains largely untuned when output plasticity is knocked out because output connections are still random.
source: In particular, feedback inhibition remains largely untuned because output connections are still random, so that Pyr neurons pool inhibition from many interneurons with different stimulus tuning.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure when output plasticity is absent.

claim: When output plasticity is knocked out, a highly significant positive correlation between input weights and RS is found in 99% of the samples.
source: When output plasticity is knocked out, we still find a highly significant positive correlation between input weights and RS in 99% of the samples (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2d-f.

claim: When output plasticity is knocked out, correlations between input and output synapses are weaker and cannot reliably be detected (2% of samples).
source: In contrast, correlations between input and output synapses are weaker and cannot reliably be detected (2% of samples).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the knock-out experiments.

claim: When output plasticity is knocked out, a correlation between output weights and RS is found in <0.01% of samples.
source: Notably, we find a correlation between output weights and RS in <0.01% of samples (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Input plasticity alone is insufficient to generate the synaptic microstructure observed in mouse V1.
source: We therefore conclude that input plasticity alone is insufficient to generate the synaptic microstructure observed in mouse V1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knock-out experiment results.

claim: When input plasticity is knocked out but output plasticity is kept intact, no formation of E/I assemblies is observed.
source: When we knock out input plasticity but keep output plasticity intact, we again observe no formation of E/I assemblies.
evidence: This claim is supported by knock-out experiment results in the model.

claim: When input plasticity is knocked out, input weights remain random.
source: The underlying reason is that input weights remain random.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model state when input plasticity is absent.

claim: When input plasticity is knocked out, interneurons collect excitation from many Pyr neurons with different preferences and maintain their initial poor stimulus selectivity.
source: Interneurons collect excitation from many Pyr neurons with different preferences, and absent plasticity on their input synapses, they maintain their initial poor stimulus selectivity (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3a-c.

claim: Because of the poor stimulus tuning of the interneurons when input plasticity is knocked out, output plasticity cannot generate stimulus-specific inhibitory inputs to the Pyr neurons.
source: Because of the poor stimulus tuning of the interneurons, output plasticity cannot generate stimulus-specific inhibitory inputs to the Pyr neurons (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d and inference from the model structure.

claim: When input plasticity is knocked out, Pyr neurons essentially receive a tonic, unspecific background inhibition that is weakly modulated by the stimulus.
source: Instead, they essentially receive a tonic, unspecific background inhibition that is weakly modulated by the stimulus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Plasticity of both the inhibitory output and the excitatory input synapses of PV interneurons is required for the formation of E/I assemblies in cortical areas without feature topography.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that plasticity of both the inhibitory output and the excitatory input synapses of PV interneurons is required for the formation of E/I assemblies in cortical areas without feature topography, such as mouse V1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knock-out experiment results.

claim: In layer 2/3 of V1, similarly tuned excitatory neurons tend to have stronger and more frequent excitatory connections.
source: In layer 2/3 of V1, similarly tuned excitatory neurons tend to have stronger and more frequent excitatory connections (Ko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: It has been hypothesised that tuned excitatory connectivity supports reliable stimulus responses by amplifying the activity of similarly tuned neurons.
source: It has been hypothesised that this tuned excitatory connectivity supports reliable stimulus responses by amplifying the activity of similarly tuned neurons (Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of co-tuned feedback inhibition could induce the opposite effect, such that similarly tuned excitatory neurons are in competition with each other.
source: However, the presence of co-tuned feedback inhibition could also induce the opposite effect, such that similarly tuned excitatory neurons are in competition with each other (Chettih and Harvey, 2019; Moreno-Bote and Drugowitsch, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: While the activity of the perturbed neuron increases, many of the other Pyr neurons are inhibited in response to the perturbation.
source: While the activity of the perturbed neuron increases, many of the other Pyr neurons are inhibited in response to the perturbation (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neurons are more strongly inhibited if they have a similar tuning to the perturbed neuron.
source: In line with recent perturbation studies (Chettih and Harvey, 2019; Sadeh and Clopath, 2020), we observe that—on average—neurons are more strongly inhibited if they have a similar tuning to the perturbed neuron (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d and citations to experimental work.

claim: Before learning, the effect of single-neuron perturbations on the network is increasingly excitatory as receptive field correlation increases.
source: The opposite holds before learning: the effect of single-neuron perturbations on the network is increasingly excitatory as receptive field correlation increases.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the perturbation experiments.

claim: Networks in which input or output plasticity was knocked out during learning show the same excitatory effect as before learning.
source: Notably, the networks in which input or output plasticity was knocked out during learning (and therefore did not develop E/I assemblies) show the same excitatory effect (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A 'blanket of inhibition' does not account for feature-specific suppression between excitatory neurons.
source: This confirms that a 'blanket of inhibition' does not account for feature-specific suppression between excitatory neurons (Sadeh and Clopath, 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiment results, supported by citation.

claim: Plasticity suppresses some of the strongest correlations, resulting in 'feature competition'.
source: Thus, plasticity suppresses some of the strongest correlations, resulting in 'feature competition' which is believed to aid sensory processing (Lochmann et al., 2012; Moreno-Bote and Drugowitsch, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citations.

claim: The stimulus-specific feedback inhibition that emerges in the model captures the paradoxical suppression of similarly tuned excitatory neurons observed in single-cell perturbation experiments.
source: In summary, the stimulus-specific feedback inhibition that emerges in the model also captures the paradoxical suppression of similarly tuned excitatory neurons observed in single-cell perturbation experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiment results.

claim: The development of E/I assemblies similar to those observed in mouse V1 can be driven by a homeostatic form of plasticity of the incoming and outgoing synapses of inhibitory interneurons.
source: Here, we used a computational model to show that the development of E/I assemblies similar to those observed in mouse V1 (Znamenskiy et al., 2018) or zebrafish olfactory areas (Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018) can be driven by a homeostatic form of plasticity of the incoming and outgoing synapses of inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by the modeling results.

claim: Input and output plasticity in interneurons must act in synergy for stimulus-specific feedback inhibition to develop.
source: Based on the results of virtual knock-out experiments, we suggest that, on their own, input or output plasticity of interneurons are insufficient to explain the Pyr-PV microcircuitry in mouse V1 and that input and output plasticity in interneurons must act in synergy for stimulus-specific feedback inhibition to develop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knock-out experiment results.

claim: Stimulating single excitatory cells paradoxically suppresses similarly tuned neurons in mouse visual cortex.
source: To investigate how the presence of E/I assemblies affects interactions between excitatory neurons, we mimicked a perturbation experiment and found that—as in mouse visual cortex—stimulating single excitatory cells paradoxically suppresses similarly tuned neurons (Chettih and Harvey, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work and comparison with model results.

claim: Activity-dependent plasticity can refine inhibitory circuits to actively shape cortical computations.
source: Our findings suggest that, by driving the development of tuned feedback inhibition, plasticity of interneurons can fundamentally shape cortical processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall modeling results.

claim: Plasticity of input synapses is required for interneurons to acquire a stimulus selectivity.
source: Plasticity of input synapses is required for interneurons to acquire a stimulus selectivity, whereas plasticity of output synapses can exploit interneuron selectivity to shape inhibitory currents onto excitatory cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knock-out experiment results.

claim: Plasticity of output synapses can exploit interneuron selectivity to shape inhibitory currents onto excitatory cells.
source: Plasticity of input synapses is required for interneurons to acquire a stimulus selectivity, whereas plasticity of output synapses can exploit interneuron selectivity to shape inhibitory currents onto excitatory cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knock-out experiment results.

claim: The output plasticity derived for the recurrent network is very similar to a previously suggested form of inhibitory plasticity.
source: The output plasticity we derived for our recurrent network is very similar to a previously suggested form of inhibitory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011; Sprekeler, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited previous work.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity rules for inhibitory synapses are now used regularly in computational studies to stabilise model circuits.
source: Homeostatic plasticity rules for inhibitory synapses are now used regularly in computational studies to stabilise model circuits (Vogels et al., 2011; Hennequin et al., 2017; Landau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A theoretically grounded approach for the plasticity of excitatory input synapses onto inhibitory neurons is missing.
source: In contrast, a theoretically grounded approach for the plasticity of excitatory input synapses onto inhibitory neurons is missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Homeostatic changes in excitatory synapses onto interneurons in response to lesions or sensory deprivation have been reported.
source: Homeostatic changes in excitatory synapses onto interneurons in response to lesions or sensory deprivation have been reported (Keck et al., 2011; Takesian et al., 2013; Kuhlman et al., 2013), but the specific mechanisms and functions of this form of interneuron plasticity are not resolved.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The plasticity rule derived for the input synapses of interneurons effectively changes the selectivity of those neurons according to the demands of the Pyr cells.
source: The plasticity rule we derived for the input synapses of interneurons effectively changes the selectivity of those neurons according to the demands of the Pyr cells, that is, such that the interneurons can best counteract deviations of Pyr activity from the target.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the derived plasticity rule.

claim: The local approximation of the gradient produces qualitatively similar results to the full gradient rules.
source: Here, we used a local approximation of the gradient, backpropagation rules, which produces qualitatively similar results, and which we interpret as a recurrent variant of feedback alignment, applied to the specific task of a stimulus-specific E/I balance (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Akrout et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of results from different plasticity rules.

claim: The task of balancing excitation by feedback inhibition favours symmetric connections.
source: The intuition why this replacement is reasonable is the following: The task of balancing excitation by feedback inhibition favours symmetric connections, because excitatory cells that strongly drive a particular PV interneuron should receive a strong feedback connection in return.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the nature of E/I balance.

claim: E/I balance favours a positive correlation between the incoming and outgoing synapses of PV neurons.
source: Therefore, E/I balance favours a positive correlation between the incoming and outgoing synapses of PV neurons and thus the two weight matrices will be aligned in a final balanced state (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Akrout et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by citations.

claim: In PV dendrites, postsynaptic sodium or calcium concentrations are expected to diffuse more broadly than in spiny neurons due to the lack of spines.
source: Due to the lack of spines in PV dendrites, both are expected to diffuse more broadly in the dendritic arbor than in spiny neurons (Hu et al., 2014; Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007) and may thus provide a signal for overall dendritic excitatory currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and inference from structural properties.

claim: In PV interneurons, NMDA receptors are enriched in excitatory feedback relative to feedforward connections.
source: Notably, in PV interneurons, NMDA receptors are enriched in excitatory feedback relative to feedforward connections (Le Roux et al., 2013), suggesting those two sources of excitation are differentially treated on the postsynaptic side.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors interferes with Hebbian long-term plasticity in some excitatory synapses onto interneurons.
source: Blocking NMDA receptors interferes with Hebbian long-term plasticity in some of these synapses (Lamsa et al., 2007; Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007), as does a block of excitatory input (Le Roux et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: NMDAR-dependent plasticity in Pyr → PV synapses is expressed postsynaptically and seems to require presynaptic activation.
source: Furthermore, NMDAR-dependent plasticity in Pyr → PV synapses is expressed postsynaptically and seems to require presynaptic activation (Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The combination of BCM plasticity in Pyr → PV synapses with homeostatic inhibitory plasticity in the PV → Pyr synapses showed complex dynamics and often did not converge to a steady state.
source: However, in our hands, the combination of BCM plasticity in Pyr → PV synapses with homeostatic inhibitory plasticity in the PV → Pyr synapses showed complex dynamics, an analysis of which is beyond the scope of this article. In particular, this combination of rules often did not converge to a steady state, probably for the following reason.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results.

claim: BCM rules tend to make the postsynaptic neuron as stimulus-selective as possible.
source: BCM rules tend to make the postsynaptic neuron as stimulus-selective as possible.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of BCM plasticity rules.

claim: Both Pyr → PV and PV→ Pyr plasticity have been studied in slice.
source: Both Pyr → PV and PV→ Pyr plasticity have been studied in slice (for reviews, see, e.g., Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007; Vogels et al., 2013), but mostly in isolation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The model did not include stimulus-specific feedforward inhibition.
source: First, we did not include stimulus-specific feedforward inhibition, because the focus lay on the formation of stimulus-specific feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design choices.

claim: The model includes only one class of interneurons.
source: Second, we neglected much of the complexity of cortical interneuron circuits by including only one class of interneurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model design choices.

claim: PV interneurons provide local feedback inhibition.
source: We interpret these interneurons as PV interneurons, given that PV interneurons provide local feedback inhibition (Hu et al., 2014) and show a stimulus-selective circuitry akin to E/I assemblies (Znamenskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: PV-expressing (basket) cells are a prime candidate for the classical feedback model of E/I balance.
source: With their peri-somatic targets on Pyr cells, PV-expressing (basket) cells are also a prime candidate for the classical feedback model of E/I balance (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work and knowledge of PV cell properties.

claim: Similarly tuned Pyr cells tend to be recurrently connected.
source: Similarly tuned Pyr cells tend to be recurrently connected (Cossell et al., 2015; Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013), in line with the notion that excitatory cells with similar tuning mutually excite each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: A recent perturbation experiment demonstrates feature-specific suppression between Pyr cells with similar tuning.
source: This notion is questioned by a recent perturbation experiment demonstrating feature-specific suppression between Pyr cells with similar tuning (Chettih and Harvey, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Feature-specific suppression requires strong and tuned connections between excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: It has been suggested that this apparently paradoxical effect requires strong and tuned connections between excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Sadeh and Clopath, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Feature competition may be beneficial for stimulus processing by generating a sparser and more efficient representation of the stimuli.

claim: In rodents, stimulus tuning of inhibitory currents occurs later in development than that of excitation.
source: Given that in rodents, stimulus tuning of inhibitory currents occurs later in development than that of excitation (Dorrn et al., 2010), we expect that in juvenile mice single-cell perturbations would not cause feature-specific suppression but amplification due to excitatory recurrence and unspecific feedback inhibition.
